\section[Practice]{Synthesis — saying what people do}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-sintesis-trabajo}



\begin{quote}
One word English needs after \emph{is} and Spanish leaves out. Which? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three chapters ago \emph{ser} was a verb with nothing to sit in front of. Now:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{Soy profesor.} & I am a teacher. \\
\emph{Ella es estudiante.} & She is a student. \\
\emph{Somos artistas.} & We are artists. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And two of those words you did not memorise. You \textbf{built} \emph{estudiante} from \emph{estudiar}, and you \textbf{read} \emph{artista} off English.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the two endings are worth}]
Neither ending is a word. Each is a \textbf{machine} that makes words, which is why they outrun any vocabulary list:

\begin{quote}
\emph{-ante} $\leftrightarrow$ \textbf{-ant} · \emph{-ista} $\leftrightarrow$ \textbf{-ist}
\end{quote}

Both are also invariant — one form for a man or a woman — so you never have to choose. Only the article moves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Soy} — and what you actually are
  \item \emph{¿Y tú?}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Two endings that name a person. (\emph{\textbf{-ante}} and \emph{\textbf{-ista}}.) What do both skip after \emph{ser}? (\emph{\textbf{un}}/\emph{\textbf{una}}.) And which of them changes for a woman? (\textbf{Neither}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
